verdicts.rewritten_summary: BBC (Aug 2024): the beaten body of Abujan trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. For this record: a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

The Dial (Feb 2025): six months after Abuja Area Mama's killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. For this record: impunity is documented — police response to a trans victim's killing produced no arrests half a year on.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. For this record: current (2026) official foreign-office warning aimed squarely at LGBT+ visitors.

TimesLIVE (Mar 2025): a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; the SSMPA is described by those affected as a 'weaponised' law creating a climate of hostility. For this record: police extortion and violence against perceived-gay people, with the specific bribe amount and injury.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024), marking 10 years of the SSMPA: the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed. For this record: a decade-outcome assessment of the national criminalisation law, not just its text.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Apr 2024): 'kito' gangs entrap LGBTQ+ Nigerians via Grindr and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing; community counters with exposure forums (one admin's alert page drawing 43,000 followers) and sting operations. For this record: documented app-based luring crime specifically targeting queer people, relevant to a visitor using dating apps.

UK Home Office CPIN on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026): same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; Sharia law in all 12 northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. For this record: current official UK-government assessment of penalties, including the north/Sharia overlay.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: HRW report (Oct 2016) 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe': the SSMPA reaches far beyond marriage — it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any 'public show of same sex amorous relationship', and gay organisations, with punishments of 10-14 years' prison; the report documents police torture and arbitrary arrests under it. For this record: the scope and severity of the national law visitors fall under.
thin: no usable finding

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report on Nicaragua: documents a police/parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among significant violations. For this record: official US assessment that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International (May 2019): the post-April-2018 protest crackdown left at least 325 dead and more than 2,000 injured per the IACHR; journalist Miguel Mora describes being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay, illustrating the intersection of political repression and homophobia. For this record: documented violence context and homophobia within the repression, with the casualty figures.

PinkNews (Nov 2007): Nicaragua's new penal code, effective March 2008, repealed the 1992 sodomy law (1-3 years' imprisonment), whose vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work. For this record: dated decriminalisation — same-sex conduct not criminalised since 2008.

Human Dignity Trust history of criminalisation, Niue section: the Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May (in force June), removing 'buggery', 'attempted buggery' and 'indecent assault on males' — offences under ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code carrying up to 10 years. The law was inherited from New Zealand via 1901 annexation, retained on self-governance in 1974, and survived New Zealand's own 1986 decriminalisation (which changed NZ law only). For this record: documented legal decriminalisation and its colonial-law chain.

GayLawNet Niue laws page: age of majority is 21 for men and 19 for women under the Niue Act 1966 (Part 21, Marriage of Minors); the age of consent was reportedly equalised in May 2011 (per ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia, May 2011); the page flags limited information available on Niue topics. For this record: dated consent-equality and the sex-asymmetric age of majority still on the books.

WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 official safety/travel page: visa requirements depend only on nationality, not gender identity — trans and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications; passports with a marker different from the birth-assigned sex or an 'X' marker are valid if officially issued, and no extra gender documents are required at the border. The Netherlands ranks #13 on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026. For this record: current official entry/border guidance for trans visitors.

Outright International Netherlands overview (updated March 2026): legal gender change still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination; the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months; the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025; compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. For this record: dated status of document-changing rules a trans visitor may care about.

Dutch government page on combating anti-LGBTIQ+ discrimination and violence: over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence — 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people — and incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism (in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation). For this record: official victimisation figures for trans people.

Government.nl (laws in force 1 July 2025): a private-member's bill (Timmermans/Bikker) puts discriminatory motive into law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. For this record: the aggravating-factor hate-crime mechanism visitors benefit from, in force since 1 July 2025.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: NL Times (Apr 2026), police figures via Transgender Netwerk: 4,800 discrimination/violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year — up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022 — with reports about transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399); COC calls it 'extremely worrying', noting only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year. For this record: quantified rise in reported anti-LGBTQ incidents with the trans-specific subset.

NL Times (Jul 2026): more than 70 people reported discrimination during the start of WorldPride Amsterdam via the RITA platform — mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants — with RITA warning the reports are 'only a fraction of the total'. For this record: documented incident volume during the 2026 Pride itself.

NL Times (Jun 2026): Amsterdam broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride — Nieuwe Kerk, Stedelijk Museum, Stadsarchief, hotels plus a central RITA location — with 1.4 million visitors expected. For this record: the incident-reporting infrastructure a visitor can actually use.

NL Times (Jun 2026): Mayor Halsema told the council Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride (police/enforcer/organiser agreements to act fast); recent Prides drew 25-45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports (vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation, serious assault), typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene. For this record: baseline Pride-period incident counts and official response posture.

OSCE/ODIHR hate-crime frameworks page for the Netherlands: Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime', while police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents (data collection by the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination, ECAD-P). For this record: the recording framework behind Netherlands hate-crime statistics.

Official Norwegian health-rights page (Gender Recognition Act): legal gender is determined by the individual's own perception of gender identity — self-declaration decided at the tax office — from age 16 alone, 6-16 with parents, under-6 only for documented congenital DSD; a 2017 regulation covers citizens resident abroad. For this record: the official, no-medical-intervention document-change route.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: NRK (May 2024, Norwegian): record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims report little trust in police, and a dedicated hate-crime group encourages reporting. For this record: rising reports with a documented, quantified drop in case clearance.

UiO C-REX research blog (Sept 2024): transphobic hostility in Norway manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists — the Nordic Resistance Movement's 2017 Kristiansand march advocated 'crushing the gay lobby', and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as 'degeneracy'. For this record: organised ideological anti-trans hostility as a movement phenomenon, not street-level risk for ordinary visitors.

UiO C-REX (June 2025), HATECYCLE study of 3,000+ survey responses from LGBTQI people: only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police — barriers include mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, and many who did report described dismissive treatment. For this record: official statistics undercount anti-LGBTQI hate crime by a wide margin.

OSCE/ODIHR frameworks page for Norway: hate crimes are defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability; any offence so motivated is recorded under the framework. For this record: the statutory definition behind Norway's hate-crime counting.

Nordisk Post (Apr 2025): Norway's Police Security Service (PST) reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride — most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act. For this record: current threat-level assessment from the security service.

Life in Norway resource page (updated Nov 2020): Norwegians generally hold liberal attitudes toward LGBT people; Norway was among the first countries with anti-discrimination laws; directory of national resources (FRI, Skeiv Ungdom, Transgender Association, Oslo Pride). For this record: social-climate context and the support-directory landscape.

HRW (Feb 2024): calls on Nepal's government to urgently create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents — illustrating that despite progressive rulings, no straightforward document-change process exists (photo shows a Kathmandu trans woman holding her 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender). For this record: official-observer statement on the documentary-recognition gap.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021; changing markers to 'female'/'male' has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams. For this record: the landmark ruling and the pre-ruling barrier path, dated.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns policy. For this record: documented doctrine-versus-implementation gap.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024) on trans life in Janakpur: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. For this record: ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities, dated 2024.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: The Record (Sept 25, 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: argues that despite the Constitution awarding the right to self-determine name and gender markers (2007 case), 'an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law' is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community. For this record: local-activist assessment of the gap between constitutional right and statute.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: US Mission Geneva (Mar 2011): publishes the full text of the Joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation & gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of 84 countries — Nauru is among the signatories (with Fiji, Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others). For this record: dated evidence of Nauru's diplomatic position supporting SOGI rights.

Human Truth Foundation 'LGBT Rights Across the World' (Vexen Crabtree, 2025): the Vexen LGBT Equality Index ranks Nauru 101st at -0.10, far below top-ranked Germany/Spain at 4.88 and below most Pacific neighbours. For this record: a comparative-index placement for Nauru.

The Guardian (29 May 2016), headline-level (article body did not survive retrieval — nav shell only): 'Nauru decriminalises homosexuality and suicide' — the 1899 Queensland-derived criminal code provisions repealed, replacing them including attempted-suicide provisions. For this record: the dated decriminalisation event.

Kaleidoscope Trust Nauru country page: Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016 but same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal; intersex and transgender people have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and no employment-discrimination protection for LBTI people; Nauru supported the 2011 UN HRC Joint Statement, and its last CEDAW state report (2016) contained no LBTI-specific information. For this record: the current legal-status snapshot for trans/intersex people specifically.

RNZ (17 Apr 2024), Official Information Act data: 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023 vs 161 in 2022 — a 42% rise — with police saying the figure likely understates true anti-trans hate, and a spike in the month anti-trans activist Posie Parker visited (March 2023). For this record: the quantified police dataset with the undercount caveat.

RNZ (27 Feb 2025), Counting Ourselves survey: almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders were threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the past four years, and 8% experienced deliberate physical violence — the first clear population picture of violence against these communities. For this record: survey-based prevalence figures.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: The Spinoff opinion (2 Jul 2024) by Jennifer Shields: after a spate of rainbow event cancellations and a 2023 Posie Parker protest, calls for more security for rainbow communities — noting statutory wins (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 2021 easing ID correction; Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022) alongside a worsening street climate. For this record: community-safety assessment dated mid-2024 with the recent statutory wins named.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: PrideNZ.com: archive of over 1,000 audio recordings of interviews and events from Aotearoa NZ's LGBTQIA+ communities, a rainbow timeline, over 18,000 GayNZ.com articles (2001-2017), and Homosexual Law Reform 40th-anniversary resources including Hansard transcripts of the parliamentary debates.
